title: Dispatch TUR 1: Mail Arrives from Stations That Were Never Built
summary: The Post Office has delivered twelve letters bearing stamps from an abandoned railway.
author: Clara Vale, Staff Correspondent
paragraphs: Twelve letters were delivered yesterday with postmarks from the Westmere Railway, a line whose construction was abandoned forty-three years ago. Their stamps name Hallowmere, Kingsfen, and North Wicket, stations that exist only on an architect’s drawings. The Post Office says it did not cancel the stamps and cannot establish how the letters entered its sorting room.

The Westmere scheme was approved in 1881, then defeated by a dispute over the marsh crossing. One mile of embankment and a stone bridge pier survive outside Alderwick. No rails were laid. The earliest of yesterday’s letters describes an ordinary journey: a complaint about cold tea, a note about a misplaced valise, and a child’s drawing of a train beneath a green sky.

One letter, addressed to Mrs. Ruth Harrow of Chapel Row, is signed by her daughter, Miriam. Mrs. Harrow is twenty-two and has no children. The writer claims to be eleven years old and apologizes for forgetting a birthday. Its postmark reads 17 October 1894.

“Someone has had a cruel joke at my expense,” Mrs. Harrow told this newspaper. She did not recognize the handwriting. She did recognize the nickname used for her husband in the salutation, one known at present only to the couple.

Chief Postal Examiner Bernard Pike has retained the envelopes but returned the letters to their addressees. He asks anyone receiving mail from the Westmere stations to preserve its wrapper. The Post Office will issue no further statement until it has identified the route by which this correspondence was carried.
